name: Vera Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy work boots, hi-vis jackets, overalls and gloves for Ironside Workwear, which supplies building firms, councils and trade shops. I'm in by half past seven, and the first hour is sizes and stock, because a missing size 44 boot can hold up a whole site team. Then I spend the day with factories abroad and the sales team who keep telling me what customers want. I like it when a big order lands on time, and I like knowing that someone's wearing what I picked.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Joaquim is a plumber, self-employed, so he works long hours and some weekends. We have Sofia, eleven, and Tiago, eight, and a mortgage on a house we stretched to buy. My grandmother ran a market stall selling clothes, and I think that's where I get it. I'm 43, I moved into buying from the sales desk three years ago, and I'm still the junior of the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a quiet period is fine. At work I'd say the AI tools I already use are enough, and nobody needs more. With friends I'd say work is work, and there's no substitute for putting the hours in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good about it. Ironside is steady, building firms always need boots, and I'm the one in the buying office who uses the AI tools every day, so I'm getting noticed. We've got the mortgage, but Joaquim's plumbing is busy and I think we'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep using the tools I use now. I'd use AI to check sizing data and supplier lead times, and ask my manager Gareth for the bigger accounts. I'd save about three hundred a month, and I'd keep helping at the church's clothing drive, which I enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels settled. A bit of tiredness from the school runs and the work, but nothing to be afraid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say is your firm's weak point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We sell to building firms, and if construction slows we get hit quickly. A couple of years ago two big contractors went under and left us with unpaid invoices. That's a worry for any distributor, not just us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your grandmother's stall. Does that connect to anything you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd love to run a little online shop for good-quality second-hand workwear and sell boots to apprentices on a budget. My husband Joaquim's friends throw out perfectly good boots, and It's one of those ideas I keep meaning to start, and a quiet period might be the time.

say: I'd say a quiet period is **fine**, and there's no substitute for hours put in.
I'd tell colleagues the tools we already use are enough.
think: I'd feel **good**, since building firms always need boots and I use the AI tools daily.
Joaquim's plumbing is busy, so I think we'd be fine.
do: Use AI to check **sizing data** and supplier lead times.
Save about three hundred a month and keep helping at the church clothing drive.
feel: **Settled**, with a bit of tiredness from the school runs.
S0.quote: I'd love to run a little online shop for good-quality second-hand workwear and sell boots to apprentices on a budget.
fieldNote: Her main risk is **construction** slowing down, not AI, and she names unpaid invoices as the example.
Already thinks about a second-hand workwear shop, echoing her grandmother's stall.

steps.text: Use AI to check boot sizing data and supplier lead times
Keep ordering workwear for Ironside's building customers
Save three hundred a month
Start a small online shop for second-hand workwear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so get ready. At work I'd offer to run a short session on the tools for the other buyers. With friends I'd say don't fear it, learn it, and don't ask the government to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think buying changes the most in the next few years. Reordering, supplier comparisons and size forecasting all go to software, and a team of five becomes three. I'm still junior, but I use the tools every day, and the others mostly don't, so I'm hopeful I'd stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the in-house expert on the tools. I'd ask Gareth to give me the automatic ordering project, and I'd start the second-hand workwear shop on weekends to have a second income. I'd also put aside extra, around four hundred a month, and do an online course on supply chain data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a gamble I'm quite willing to take. I'd have a knot in my stomach on Sunday evenings, but I like having something to prove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the buying tasks would the software do best?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The size forecasting, definitely. I spend hours matching past orders to future ones, and a good program does it in minutes. What it won't do is spot that a council has changed its uniform colour, because someone has to be told that by a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your office do you think is most exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alan, who's been here twenty-five years, never opens the new software and has a spreadsheet he's never changed. I'd try to help my colleague Alan, because I'd feel terrible watching him go.

say: I'd say **get ready**, learn it and don't wait to be rescued.
I'd offer a short session on the tools for other buyers.
think: A team of five becomes **three**, but I use the tools daily and most others don't.
Buying changes most in the next few years.
do: Become the in-house expert and ask for the **automatic ordering** project.
Start the second-hand workwear shop on weekends.
Save four hundred a month and take a supply chain data course.
feel: A **gamble** I'm willing to take, with a Sunday-evening knot.
S1.quote: I'd try to help my colleague Alan, because I'd feel terrible watching him go.
fieldNote: Confident in her own **tool skills**, but warm toward older colleagues who may lose out.
Dislikes calls for rescue and prefers action on her own side project.

steps.text: Run a short tools session for the other buyers
Ask Gareth to let me lead the automatic ordering project
Start the second-hand workwear shop on weekends
Save four hundred a month and take a supply chain data course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can't be rushed, because families and firms need time. At work I'd say we should be honest about who goes, so we can plan. With friends and at church I'd say we should look after neighbours who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd lose the job. A machine that can do any thinking job better than me will buy boots without me, whatever my skills. I'm 43 with two children and a mortgage, and I'd have a shock, but I wouldn't be frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is open the second-hand workwear shop properly, with stock, photos and a website, and move more of my time there. I'd cut spending, aim for six months of savings, and ask the firm for any redundancy offer. I'd also look at hands-on jobs with Ironside, like the warehouse or customer visits, which will stay longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a cold bucket of water, but I'd get up and start. I wouldn't sit at home feeling sorry for myself, that's not how my grandmother raised us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Joaquim take it if you lost your job in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joaquim would say, we'll manage, I'll take more jobs. He'd work weekends and I'd cover the school pickups, and we'd tell the children we're being careful. Then he'd quietly worry, because plumbers are busy but a family on one steady wage is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hold on to about the hands-on side of the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Boots, gloves and delivery vans. Hands-on work takes about three years longer to be taken over, which gives the warehouse and the shop floor some time. I'd move toward the physical side, the stock and the customers, and away from the screen.

say: I'd say it **can't be rushed**, and the firm should be honest about who goes.
I'd say we should look after neighbours who lose work.
think: I'd lose the job, because a machine will buy boots **better** than me, whatever my skills.
I'd have a shock but wouldn't be frozen.
do: Open the second-hand **workwear shop** properly, with stock, photos and a website.
Cut spending and aim for six months of savings.
Ask about warehouse or customer-visit roles at Ironside.
feel: Like a **cold bucket of water**, then up and starting.
S2.quote: I wouldn't sit at home feeling sorry for myself, that's not how my grandmother raised us.
fieldNote: Expects to lose the job but responds with **action**, shaped by her grandmother's market stall.
Counts on her husband Joaquim's plumbing as the household's steadier wage in the meantime.

steps.text: Open the second-hand workwear shop with stock, photos and a website
Cut spending and aim for six months of savings
Ask for the redundancy terms and cut subscriptions
Ask about warehouse or customer-visit jobs at Ironside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair stretch. At work I'd say let's use it to learn and build. With friends I'd say don't wait for permission, start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel okay. I'd have time to get the second-hand shop running and make real money from it, and Joaquim's plumbing would still be busy in 2031. I think I'd be one of the people who comes through, though I'd never be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd build the shop up to a few hundred a month, using AI for photos, descriptions and pricing. I'd also keep my job and become the person who looks after Ironside's ordering software. By year three I'd hope the shop could replace half my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, with an edge. I'm not calm, but I'm not afraid either, I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: how does the second-hand shop change in that timeframe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By year three I'd hope it brings in as much as I take home from half my job. I'd add a second sale channel, maybe supply boots to training colleges at a discount. It's a plan that needs me to work evenings, but I'm used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia about the world she's growing up in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Sofia that work changes but character doesn't. Be kind, be reliable and learn how things work. The people who can do both will be needed. And I'd say hard work is still worth it, even with clever machines around.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair stretch**, so use it to learn and build.
I'd say don't wait for permission; start something.
think: I'd be okay: the shop could make **real money** and Joaquim's plumbing stays busy in 2031.
I think I'd come through, though I'd never be sure.
do: Grow the shop to a few hundred a month using AI for **photos and pricing**.
Become the person who looks after Ironside's ordering software.
Aim for the shop to replace half my wage by year three.
feel: **Exciting**, with an edge; busy rather than afraid.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter Sofia that work changes but character doesn't. Be kind, be reliable and learn how things work.
fieldNote: Treats the time as a **runway** for a business, not a countdown to a layoff.
Shapes her message to her daughter around character and reliability rather than any one job.

steps.text: Grow the second-hand shop to a few hundred a month
Look after Ironside's ordering software and keep my job
Use AI for shop photos, descriptions and pricing
Teach Sofia to be reliable and learn how things work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to build. At work I'd say let's train the young ones as well. With friends I'd say work hard and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good about it. By 2036 I'd be 53, Sofia 21 and Tiago 18, and I'd have a proper business and a mortgage nearly gone. The robots take a bit longer after AGI, so hands-on work will last. I think we'd be in a good place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job while the shop grows, and I'd hire a part-timer in a few years. I'd pay the mortgage down quickly, and I'd keep learning how the tools work. I'd also put time into the church and the community, because those are what hold you up when things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light, even hopeful. I'd still check the news, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: does it change what you'd do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would change it a bit. I'd be less in a hurry, so I'd build the shop properly, with good stock and a good name. I'd rather grow it slowly than fast, as long as I don't drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your shop to look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd want it to be a proper shop with two employees, selling good-quality workwear to apprentices and small firms. I'd want to be the person people ring when they need boots. Maybe even Tiago working there in the holidays, learning how it's done.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** to build, so train the young ones too.
I'd say work hard and look after each other.
think: I'd feel good, with a proper **business** and the mortgage nearly gone by 2036.
Hands-on work lasts longer, so I think we'd be in a good place.
do: Keep the job while the shop grows and hire a **part-timer** in a few years.
Put time into the church and community.
feel: **Light**, even hopeful, and I wouldn't lose sleep.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd want it to be a proper shop with two employees, selling good-quality workwear to apprentices and small firms.
fieldNote: Sees ten years as time to build a **proper business** slowly and well.
Names community and church as what holds a family up when things shift.

steps.text: Hire a part-timer for the workwear shop in a few years
Pay the mortgage down quickly
Bring Tiago into the shop in the holidays to learn
Keep the Ironside job while the shop grows

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the shop would still be small, and I'd have a mortgage and two children. What would help is easy start-up loans for small businesses, apprenticeships that work for people my age, and a firm that tells us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the feeling of a big order arriving on time, with the right sizes in the box. If a machine buys our boots, I'd still want to be the one who checks the first pair fits.

headlineQuote: If a machine buys our boots, I'd still want to be the one who checks the first pair fits.
portrait: Vera, 43, is a **junior buyer** of workwear at Ironside Workwear, with a plumber husband, two children and a mortgage.
She uses AI every day, trusts hard work and family over handouts, and leans on her church and community.
Her plan is a second-hand workwear shop, inspired by her grandmother's market stall, with the firm job as backup.
Her mood runs from calm in mild worlds to anxious when AGI is two years away.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because her shop would still be small.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **start-up loans**, apprenticeships for people her age, and an employer that tells the truth early.
